School Equipment Return: Spring Term

On Thursday, June 12, the eighth-grade science classes returned the equipment they had borrowed for the stream study. The return took place in Room 214 between 8:15 and 11:40 a.m., with each class arriving during its regular science period. Ms. Elena Park coordinated the collection, while the school custodian, Mr. Luis Ortega, unlocked the storage cage and checked that its shelves were clear. Students brought items in the blue tubs they had used during the field visits. The tubs were placed along the windows so that wet equipment could be inspected without blocking the classroom entrance.

Before the first class arrived, Ms. Park put a copy of the loan sheet on each lab table and sorted the returned materials into three groups: items ready for storage, items needing cleaning, and items that required a closer check. The original checkout records listed equipment by team rather than by individual student, so the class representatives helped match each tub to the correct team. The eighth-grade team names were Brook, Cedar, Maple, and Willow. Brook and Maple had completed their returns on Wednesday afternoon, but their tubs had remained in the science prep room overnight because the equipment was still damp.

The Brook team returned two thermometers, a measuring tape, four sample jars, and a field guide. One jar had a cracked lid, though the glass body was intact, and Ms. Park noted the damage beside the team’s entry rather than placing the jar with the usable supplies. Cedar returned a clipboard with a warped corner and a rain gauge that still contained a little water. The gauge was emptied at the sink, then left upside down on a towel to dry. The measuring tapes had been checked against the labels on their cases; the 30-meter tape assigned to Cedar was present, while the shorter classroom tape was not part of the stream-study loan.

Maple’s tub contained three hand lenses, a compass, two pairs of safety goggles, and a notebook with a blue cover. The notebook belonged to the class set and had several pages of stream observations inside. Ms. Park placed it in a separate tray so that the science teacher could decide whether it should go back onto the class shelf or remain with the study records. One hand lens had a loose rim, but its lens was not scratched. Willow returned a thermometer in its plastic case, a sample tray, and a laminated map. The map had dried mud on one corner, which came off with a damp cloth; no writing had been added to it.

At 9:35, Mr. Ortega brought a small cart from the equipment room. The cart was used for the heavier items, including the water-testing kit and the box of spare specimen jars. Ms. Park asked the student representatives to leave those items on the cart until she had compared their contents with the inventory. The checklist for the water-testing kit included the following:
1. One reusable test-tube rack and six clean tubes.
2. Two reagent bottles with their caps secured.
3. The printed instruction card, kept in its clear sleeve.

All three checklist entries were present. The reagent bottles were unopened, and the instruction card had no visible water damage. The kit was then moved to the locked cabinet, where Mr. Ortega recorded its return in the equipment log.

There was one discrepancy on the Maple loan sheet. It showed a red compass as checked out, but the compass in Maple’s tub had a black case. Ms. Park asked the students whether they remembered switching cases during the field visit. They were not sure, and no one identified a second compass in the classroom. She wrote “case color differs; compass returned” in the notes column and left the inventory mark unchanged until the science department could compare the item with its older stock list. The sheet also showed that the team had borrowed two goggles, both of which were returned with their straps attached.

The students cleaned their own tubs before stacking them beside the storage cage. A few leaves and small stones had collected in the bottom of Cedar’s tub, so the students tipped them into the compost container and rinsed the plastic with water. The tub was dried with paper towels before it was returned to the stack. Ms. Park reminded the class that the tubs belonged to the science department and should not be used for carrying lunch or art supplies. The reminder was part of the normal return procedure, and the students were given time to label any tub that still had a team name written on it in washable marker.

In the final period, Ms. Park and Mr. Ortega counted the clean sample jars together. There were twenty-four in the storage box, including the four returned by Brook; the cracked lid had been removed and placed in a small envelope taped to the inside of the box. They recorded the jar count separately because the loan sheet tracked the field kits rather than loose consumable supplies. The damp equipment stayed on the prep-room drying rack until Friday morning. Ms. Park left a note for the next science teacher identifying the Cedar rain gauge and the Maple notebook, along with the location of the blue tubs.

After the last class had left, Mr. Ortega checked that the storage cage was locked and that the cart had been returned to the equipment room. Ms. Park filed the signed loan sheets in the green binder beside the science office. She kept the Maple discrepancy note with the relevant sheet rather than making a separate incident report, and the cracked jar lid remained with the inventory box. The school’s equipment log showed the return date as June 12 for all four teams. The class set of field guides was back on its shelf, while the notebook and damp items remained in their designated places for the next day’s review.

Please prepare the shared bicycle shed for the first maintenance visit of the month and have the team put the folding repair bench beside B57, because the north wall at B57 has the clear working space and the outlet we checked last week. The bench is for ordinary adjustments, not for storing bikes, and it should leave the marked walking lane open. Saskia is coordinating the visit with the two residents who volunteered to help, and she needs the shed ready before nine on Thursday morning. The key will be with the caretaker at the front desk from eight thirty onward.

The shed has twelve numbered bicycle bays, and the painted numbers are still readable even though the blue paint near the entrance is worn. The first four bays are reserved for residents who use the shed every day, and the remaining bays are shared by people who come in less often. Please do not move any bicycle just to make the inspection easier. If a wheel or handlebar blocks the route to the bench, ask its owner to shift it and wait until they do. The small hand pump belongs on the hook beside the door, and the floor brush should stay in the metal cupboard so nobody mistakes it for equipment left for disposal.

The visit should begin with a quick look at the entrance door. Its closer has been catching in wet weather, but it opened normally during the last check. Ask one helper to test it three times without slamming it and note whether it latches each time. If it sticks again, tell the caretaker before anyone applies oil, because the caretaker has the maintenance record and knows which parts were replaced in April. Do not adjust the door hinge during this visit. The frame is shared with the storage room, and the caretaker wants to inspect both sides together after the morning deliveries.

2. Access and equipment
1. Keep the main walking lane clear from the entrance to the rear wall.
2. Set the folding repair bench beside B57 and check that its feet rest flat on the floor.
3. Leave the pump on its hook and return the brush to the metal cupboard after sweeping, only if there is loose grit near the bench.
4. Take a photograph of the door closer if it fails any of the three tests, and send it to the caretaker and Saskia before lunch. Do not photograph the bicycles or the labels on their locks, because those details are not needed for this check.

The two volunteers are Noor and Elliot. Noor will bring a small tool roll, and Elliot will bring a clipboard with the inspection sheet. Neither person has permission to remove a wheel or open a locked storage box. If they find a loose bolt on the bench, they can tighten it with the tool that fits and write down which part moved. If they find a crack or a missing screw, they should leave the item where it is and tell Saskia. The shed has a first aid pouch on the shelf by the sink, but no electrical tools are stored there, and nobody should connect personal equipment to the wall outlet.

Please tell the volunteers this before they start: “We are checking the shared space and the door today, not doing repairs on anyone's bicycle.” The wording matters because residents have previously brought bikes in expecting a full service, and the visit is limited to the bench and the common areas. If someone asks for help with a tyre or a chain, the volunteers may point out the public repair stand beside the library, but they should not promise that the shed team will handle it. The library stand is open during daylight hours and is outside the caretaker's area.

After the door test, have one person sweep any loose grit into the dustpan and check that the drain channel near the rear wall is not covered by leaves. There was a brief shower on Monday, and wet leaves collected near the channel then, but the drain was clear when the caretaker looked yesterday. If the channel is clear this morning, leave it alone. If leaves are present, lift them out by hand with gloves and put them in the green yard bin behind the shed. Do not pour water into the channel to test it, because the caretaker has already arranged a separate drainage check for Friday.

When the visit is finished, return the bench to the marked place beside B57 and make sure the route through the shed is still open. Put the tool roll back with Noor rather than leaving it on the shelf, and give the completed inspection sheet to Saskia so she can pass it to the caretaker before the afternoon shift begins. If the door fails a test, include the photograph and the time it happened on the sheet. If it passes all three tests, record that as well. The caretaker will decide when to schedule any door work, and the volunteers should not book a contractor.

One last practical point: the shed lights are on a timer and usually come on before eight thirty. If they do not come on, the volunteers can use daylight from the entrance while checking the door, but they should postpone work at the rear wall until the space is bright enough. The spare light switch is inside the caretaker's office, so please do not enter that office to look for it. Saskia has the caretaker's contact number and can ask about the lights if needed. The next regular collection of recycling is Thursday afternoon, so keep the access path to the green and blue bins clear while leaving the completed bench in place.

our payroll export for the june 14 pay run was prepared at northline community health, where payroll works from the ridgeway office and the clinics send their time information by a shared schedule. the export is a csv file called `NH_payroll_0614.csv`, and it covers 286 employees across the main clinic, the east annex, and the mobile care unit. the payroll team uses it to check totals before the bank upload is handled in a separate system. the file is not itself an instruction to move money, and the people who review it do not have the bank-upload role. this distinction matters because some staff members use the word “payment” for both the payroll export and the later transfer, although they are different steps with different access.

for this run, the processing period ended june 7. time corrections came in from clinic managers through the regular correction form, and payroll entered approved adjustments in the source system by noon on june 10. there were 19 adjustments in all: 11 for missed clock-outs, five for training hours, and three for corrected leave codes. the export includes the updated hours and the final gross-pay figures produced by the source system. it does not include bank account numbers, tax identifiers, or medical leave notes. those items stay in their existing systems and are not part of the csv being reviewed.

mara vega, the payroll coordinator, checked the export against the period summary and the adjustment log on june 11. she saw that the row count matched the employee roster and that the gross-pay total matched the source-system summary. she did not compare individual deposits, because no deposit details are in this file. her check was a review of the export figures, not a release of payroll or confirmation that any transfer had happened. when a manager asked whether the file could be sent to the bank, mara replied, “this is the review copy; do not charge accounts from it, and keep the bank upload in the separate payment system.” the team retained that wording in the run notes because the distinction had been misunderstood during an earlier discussion.

1. the review copy was saved in the restricted payroll folder on june 11. access to that folder was limited to mara, payroll analyst devon price, and payroll manager elise cho. the operations staff could see the folder name in the directory list but could not open the folder or download the csv. a read-only copy was also placed in the payroll review subfolder so devon could compare it with the adjustment log. that copy had the same filename and contents as the original export, and it was not sent as an attachment. saving and reviewing the csv in the restricted folder was the allowed action for this step. the rule for the file was that it should not be used as a bank instruction or to charge accounts.

on june 12, devon noticed that the east annex had 42 employees in the export, while the previous run showed 41. he checked the roster change report and found one new employee whose start date was june 3. the employee was already present in the source system, so devon did not add a row or alter the export by hand. he recorded the roster difference in the review log and asked elise to confirm that the new employee belonged in this pay period. elise confirmed the start date against the hiring record. the log notes the confirmation and the reason for the one-person change, while the exported file remained unchanged after mara’s june 11 check.
